title: Waking
hook: Modeh Ani before your feet touch the floor, every day this week
tomorrow: a fight last night. how do you start the day clean?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a rule of three lines: fixed enough to keep, alive enough to mean. Today, the first line of the morning, and the first words of it.
screen: `A RULE OF THREE LINES.` → `THE FIRST LINE OF THE MORNING.`

segments.voice: The alarm goes off, and a hand finds the phone before the eyes are fully open. Headlines, messages, someone else's vacation. The day has started, and it started with everybody else's voice. Jewish tradition puts something in that gap, before your feet even touch the floor. One short Hebrew sentence, said lying down or sitting on the edge of the bed, eyes still heavy. They're called Modeh Ani, and they are the first words of the day.
screen: `A HAND FINDS THE PHONE.` → `EVERYBODY ELSE'S VOICE.` → `BEFORE YOUR FEET TOUCH THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's what Modeh Ani says, in plain English. I give thanks before You, living and lasting King, for You have returned my soul to me, with compassion. Great is Your faithfulness. A woman says modah ani; a man, modeh ani. Same thanks. Notice what it's built around. Not a request, not a plan for the day. Thanks, for something that happened while you weren't paying attention: you woke up. Tradition reads sleep as a small letting go, and waking as the soul handed back. You didn't earn it overnight. It was returned. And the last words, great is Your faithfulness, come straight from the book of Lamentations, a book of grief, where the writer says of God's mercies: "They are new every morning; great is Thy faithfulness." One to tell a friend tonight: the morning thank-you borrows its ending from a book of grief. It means the thanks isn't only for good mornings. Here's a small detail people notice: Modeh Ani has no name of God in it, only You. That's why, by custom, it can be said right away, before washing, still in bed. It's made to be the very first thing. Some families teach it to toddlers, sung, before they can read. So this week, the line is easy to carry. Before the phone, before the floor: first words, thanks.
screen: `I GIVE THANKS: MY SOUL RETURNED.` · `SLEEP LETS GO; WAKING HANDS IT BACK.` · `NEW EVERY MORNING.` · `NO NAME OF GOD, SO SAY IT IN BED.` · then, large: `FIRST WORDS, THANKS.`

segments.voice: Sit on the edge of your chair the way you'd sit on the edge of a bed, feet just lifted off the floor, hands resting on your knees. If you say it, say modeh ani or modah ani, softly, or the English; if not, say thank you for waking up, out loud. Then set both feet down slowly and feel the floor meet you.
screen: `THE EDGE OF THE BED.` · `FEET LIFTED.` · `FIRST WORDS, THEN THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Waking: Modeh Ani, the first words of a Jewish morning. Thanks for a soul handed back, before your feet touch the floor.

howItsDone: On waking, Jews traditionally say Modeh Ani before getting out of bed (modah ani for women); children often learn it as a short song, and it is said before washing because it contains no name of God.
